name: Belchite old town (Pueblo Viejo)
text: During the Republican Zaragoza offensive the Army of the East under General Sebastián Pozas, with the XI and XV International Brigades, turned on Belchite when the drive on Zaragoza stalled. Some 5,000 people were inside the town, around 2,000 of them troops and the rest civilians. Republican troops went in on 1 September and fought house by house, and the town fell on 6 September. The fighting at Belchite cost the Nationalists about 2,000 dead and more than 2,400 captured. After the war Franco left the ruins as a monument and built a new Belchite next to them. The Trujal, once a Nationalist memorial inside the ruins, now honours all who died in the battle.
look: Shell-scarred churches of San Martín de Tours and San Agustín, the Torre del Reloj, the Arco de San Roque and streets of roofless houses. There is also the Trujal memorial.
plan: Entry is by guided tour only. Buy tickets at the tourist office (C/ Becú 2, new town) or at tienda.belchite.es and collect them 30 min before the tour. Daytime tours run daily (€6) and night tours on Fri–Sat (€10).
disputed: Casualty and garrison figures vary between sources. The numbers here follow English Wikipedia and cover only the town, not the whole offensive.

name: Teruel Civil War shelters & old town (Plaza del Torico)
text: Teruel was at the heart of the war's harshest battle. On 15 December 1937 the Republican Army of the Levante under Hernández Saravia, with Líster's and El Campesino's divisions, encircled the city, and by 21 December they were inside it. Colonel Domingo Rey d'Harcourt's garrison held out in the Civil Government building, the Bank of Spain, the Santa Clara convent and the Seminary. Many civilians sheltered with them. Rey d'Harcourt surrendered on 8 January 1938. The battle was fought in blizzards, with temperatures down to about −18°C. Franco's counter-offensive under Aranda and Varela retook the ruined city on 22 February 1938. Both sides together lost more than 100,000 men killed, wounded, sick or captured.
look: Underground air-raid shelters from the war lie beneath the old-town centre. Rebuilt buildings around the Plaza del Torico stand on the ground where the siege was fought street by street.
plan: The shelters can usually be visited on guided tours run by the city. Check times and tickets at Teruel's tourist office before you go. The old town is easily covered on foot.
disputed: Casualty totals for Teruel differ widely: about 110,000 in the Battle of Teruel article and about 140,000 in the Teruel city article. The exact entrance point of the shelters was not verified.

name: Ruta Orwell – Monte Irazo & Las Tres Huegas (Sierra de Alcubierre)
text: From late 1936 the Aragon front ran across the bare Sierra de Alcubierre. Anarchist and POUM militia columns faced Nationalist positions such as San Simón, and the front hardly moved for more than a year. The British writer George Orwell served here with the POUM militia, first on Monte Pucero and then on the crest of Monte Irazo until 16 February 1937. He described the cold, the lice and the stalemate in Homage to Catalonia (1938). The Republicans held these positions until the Nationalist Aragon offensive broke the front in March 1938. A monument to the Nationalist side from the 1940s stands on San Simón (699 m).
look: Excavated and rebuilt Republican trenches, rifle pits, an observation post, shelters and a bivouac line with barbed wire on Monte Irazo. Las Tres Huegas has a rebuilt camp with a command post, kitchens, cisterns and a cave shelter. Panels explain the sites.
plan: Monte Irazo is reached by a 1.5 km dirt track from the A-129 at about km 35.5 between Leciñena and Alcubierre. Las Tres Huegas is at about km 33.5. The sites are open-air and free. Bring water and sturdy shoes.

name: Pozos de Caudé memorial (Concud)
text: The site is a well about 50 m deep beside an old inn on the Teruel–Zaragoza road, near Concud. From July 1936 until the Republican encirclement of Teruel in December 1937, people held for their political views in Nationalist-held Teruel were shot here and thrown into the well. When the well was full, pits were dug nearby. It is one of the largest execution sites of the rearguard repression in Aragon. Families and associations campaigned for decades to have the victims remembered and identified.
look: The covered mouth of the well, a wall of plaques put up by families and several memorials, one of them to anarchist victims.
plan: The memorial is by the N-234 just west of Teruel and is open-access. Please treat it as a grave site.
disputed: Victim numbers are not established and estimates vary greatly. The TracesOfWar entry says killings were committed by both sides as Teruel changed hands, but most sources attribute the well killings to the Nationalist rearguard.

name: El Muletón (Tortajada)
text: El Muletón is a steep hill north-west of Teruel that commands the road north and the Alfambra valley. The Nationalists fortified it as part of the city's outer defences, with trenches, shelters and a concrete cistern. Republican troops stormed it early in the December 1937 offensive, and it became a key position in the struggle for Teruel. Heavy fighting went on around it in January 1938, when Nationalist artillery and aircraft pounded the Republican lines. It is one of the best places to understand the ground around the city.
look: A command post, the concrete cistern and trench lines. Shell and bomb craters from January 1938 are still visible near the Gilochas ravine.
plan: The hill is reached from Tortajada, a few km north of Teruel. It is an open hillside with rough walking, so wear boots.

name: Battle of the Alfambra interpretation centre (Villarquemado)
text: In early February 1938 Franco's army broke the Republican front north of Teruel in the Alfambra valley. It overran the area of Celadas, Alfambra, Villarquemado and Camañas and made thousands of prisoners. The attack included a charge by Nationalist cavalry, often called one of the last great cavalry charges in Western Europe. The breakthrough cut off the Republican salient north of the city and prepared the retaking of Teruel two weeks later. The centre explains the battle with maps, photographs, panels and objects, and links it to trenches in the surrounding countryside.
look: Exhibition of maps, photos and military objects. Surviving trenches and positions nearby are part of the 'Atrinchérate' route.
plan: The centre is at C/ la Virgen 11, Villarquemado (tel. 978 867 006), about 24 km north of Teruel. Opening is limited, so ring the council or check villarquemado.es before you go.

name: Civil War in Aragon interpretation centre (Robres)
text: Robres lay just behind the Republican side of the Sierra de Alcubierre front, which was held from 1936 to 1938 by anarchist (CNT-FAI) and POUM militia columns and later by the Popular Army. The village's centre for the interpretation, study and documentation of the Civil War in Aragon covers the militia war and the static front. It also covers the collectives and social revolution in the Republican rear, and the Nationalist breakthrough of March 1938. It pairs naturally with the Ruta Orwell trenches in the hills nearby.
look: Exhibition rooms with panels, photographs, weapons and everyday objects from the front, plus a documentation centre.
plan: Opening hours are limited, often weekends or by appointment, so contact Robres council or Los Monegros tourism first. Combine it with the Ruta Orwell, about 15 minutes away by car.

name: Quinto – Purburel / Cabezo de la Nariz trenches
text: Quinto was a fortified Nationalist outpost on the Ebro that had been on the front for a year. Its main strongpoint was on the Purburel and Cabezo de la Nariz hills, held by about 650 men behind wire, trenches and concrete works. On 24–26 August 1937 the Republican 35th Division, including the XV International Brigade with its British, American (Lincoln) and Dimitrov battalions, stormed the town and the hills. The last defenders on Cabezo de la Nariz surrendered on 26 August. Quinto then served as a Republican headquarters until March 1938.
look: About 250 m of excavated earth trenches, rifle pits, dugouts and an observation post with interpretation panels. There are views over the Ebro plain.
plan: The site is about 2 km from Quinto town centre (4.5 km by the marked trail). It is open-access, and the council also offers guided visits.
disputed: The garrison figures are estimates from the local visit guide, with wide margins (±150).

name: Torrero Cemetery memorials (Zaragoza)
text: Zaragoza fell to the military rising on 19 July 1936 without a fight and became the Nationalists' main base on the Aragon front. In the city, repression was carried out mainly at the walls of Torrero cemetery, where thousands were shot in the war and post-war years. In 1979 the remains of about 2,500 victims were found beneath a cemetery walkway. The following year Zaragoza's first democratic mayor, Ramón Sainz de Varanda, dedicated a monument over their common grave. The same cemetery holds a Nationalist memorial chapel with graves of the fallen of the other side.
look: The 1980 memorial over the mass grave near Joaquín Costa's mausoleum, later memorial walls with victims' names, and the Nationalist memorial chapel with graves set in its walls.
plan: The cemetery is in the south of the city (C/ Fray Julián Garcés) and is open daily during cemetery hours. Entry is free. Please be respectful.
disputed: The total number of people executed at Torrero is still researched and debated. About 2,500 refers only to the remains found in 1979.

name: Basílica del Pilar – the unexploded bombs (Zaragoza)
text: Early in the war a Republican aircraft attacked Nationalist-held Zaragoza and dropped bombs on the Basilica of Our Lady of the Pillar, Spain's great Marian shrine. Three bombs hit the church and none exploded. Nationalist propaganda presented this as a miracle, and the event became a strong symbol of the religious meaning Franco's side gave its war. Two of the bombs are still displayed inside the basilica.
look: Two defused bombs hang on a pillar inside the basilica. There is also a mark of the damage on the ceiling vaults.
plan: The basilica is open daily with free entry, so visit outside Mass times. The bombs are near the Holy Chapel of the Pillar.
disputed: Wikipedia says only that the bombs fell during the war. The date of 3 August 1936 is the one commonly given but was not confirmed from a second source here.

name: Alcañiz air-raid shelter
text: Alcañiz council built this shelter in 1937 for about 230 residents of the Almudines quarter. On 3 March 1938, at 16:10, bombers of the Italian Aviazione Legionaria, flying for the Nationalists, attacked the town centre and market area, although the front was more than 70 km away. It was one of the deadliest raids on a town in Aragon. The raid came days before the Nationalist Aragon offensive swept through the Bajo Aragón. The shelter now holds a permanent exhibition about the raid and its victims.
look: An original underground shelter gallery with a permanent exhibition on the 1938 bombing.
plan: The shelter is between C/ Teniente Moore and C/ Santo Domingo in the old town. Visits last about 30 minutes and are run by Alcañiz council or the tourist office, so check opening days before you go.
disputed: The death toll is uncertain: sources give between about 300 and more than 500 dead and missing. Italian authorship is widely stated but was not confirmed from the source checked here.

name: Barbastro – Claretian Martyrs Museum
text: Barbastro stayed in Republican hands after the rising. In the first weeks of the war anarchist militias carried out one of the worst killings of clergy in the Republican zone here. The dead included 51 Claretian missionaries, mostly young seminarians, as well as Benedictines, Piarists, cathedral canons and diocesan priests. Bishop Florentino Asensio was also killed. The diocese lost a larger share of its clergy than any other in Spain. The 51 Claretians were beatified in 1992. A museum in the Claretian house tells their story.
look: The museum in the Claretian community's house, with the seminarians' letters and belongings and a crypt with their remains.
plan: Barbastro is about 50 km east of Huesca. Opening hours were not verified, so contact the Claretians or Barbastro tourist office in advance.
disputed: The museum's exact address and hours were not verified, and the coordinates are the town centre. Figures follow Wikipedia.

name: Codo – battle of the Montserrat requetés
text: At the start of the Zaragoza offensive the Republican 25th Division attacked the small village of Codo, between Belchite and Quinto. It was held by the Tercio de Nuestra Señora de Montserrat, a battalion of Catalan Carlist volunteers (requetés) of about 200 men, together with other troops. Encircled on 24 August, the defenders fought on until the survivors broke out on 25 August. The battalion lost about 150 killed and ceased to exist as a fighting unit. Its 1st and 2nd companies later received the Laureate Cross of San Fernando.
look: A small village rebuilt after the war, with a commemorative cross to the fallen requetés.
plan: Codo is a short drive from Belchite and is easily combined with Belchite and Quinto. The cross and village are freely accessible.
disputed: The exact position of the memorial cross was not verified, so the coordinates are the village centre. Casualty numbers come from pro-requeté sources.

name: Quinto – El Piquete church
text: The old parish church of the Assumption, called 'El Piquete', stands on the Cerro de la Corona above Quinto. In August 1937 about 300 Nationalist defenders turned it into a fortress, and civilians also took refuge inside. The XV International Brigade and other Republican units took it after bitter house-to-house fighting and artillery fire, and the western face of the tower was heavily damaged. The fighting destroyed most of the town, which was rebuilt after the war by the Francoist regions-devastated agency.
look: The battle-scarred church on its hill. Inside, restoration uncovered 18th-century mummified burials ('las momias de Quinto'), now displayed there.
plan: Visits are run by Quinto council, so check times locally. Combine it with the Purburel trenches.
disputed: Coordinates were converted from the UTM grid reference in the local guide (30T 709150 4589050).

name: Estrecho Quinto bunker (Huesca front)
text: After July 1936, Nationalist-held Huesca was almost surrounded by Republican columns, and the siege lines around the city lasted until March 1938. In late 1936 Republican forces under Colonel Villalba built this machine-gun bunker at Estrecho Quinto to control the Huesca–Barbastro road. It formed one complex with the positions at Montearagón castle and trench lines nearby. The Huesca front saw costly Republican attacks, above all the June 1937 Huesca offensive, when General Lukács of the XII International Brigade was killed. George Orwell was wounded on this front in May 1937.
look: A well-preserved concrete machine-gun bunker beside the old road, with trench remains on the nearby hills.
plan: It is east of Huesca near Tierz and Loporzano. A quick stop of 15–30 min, freely accessible. There is a marked walking route from Siétamo.

name: Montearagón castle (Huesca siege lines)
text: The 11th-century castle-abbey of Montearagón stands on a hill east of Huesca. From 1936 to 1938 it was part of the Republican ring around Nationalist-held Huesca, together with the Estrecho Quinto bunker below. Its commanding views over the city made it an important observation and defensive position for the Republican columns and, later, the Popular Army. The front moved away only when the Nationalist offensive of March 1938 broke the siege lines.
look: Massive medieval walls on a hilltop with views over Huesca and the siege ground. Civil War remains are nearby.
plan: Guided visits only (about €5), in several sessions a day. Book by phone (622 573 497) or online.
disputed: The castle's own site gives no Civil War details. Its role is taken from the Aragon heritage entry for Estrecho Quinto.

name: Alto de la Torana bunker (Corbalán)
text: East of Teruel the Republicans built a fortified line on the heights around Corbalán after the militia columns reached the area in summer 1936. Alto de la Torana was its strongest point. It controlled the old road into Teruel and was flanked by the neighbouring heights of El Tocón and El Chopo. The nearby Cabigordo trenches saw heavy fighting in the last phase of the Battle of Teruel. The site has been restored as part of the 'Atrinchérate' route of 17 Civil War sites around Teruel.
look: A machine-gun post in excellent condition with iron reinforcement, parallel trenches, a concrete-walled shelter and a deep command bunker cut into the rock.
plan: It is by the A-226 near Corbalán, with parking and interpretation panels. The 'Atrinchérate' app adds audio and augmented-reality content.

name: Bielsa museum – the Bielsa Pocket
text: When the Nationalist Aragon offensive broke the front in spring 1938, the Republican 43rd Division under Antonio Beltrán ('El Esquinazau') was cut off in the high Pyrenean valley of Bielsa. For about two months the division held the 'Bolsa de Bielsa' pocket against far larger forces while thousands of civilians crossed the passes into France. In mid-June 1938 the soldiers followed them. Most of the men went back to Republican Catalonia to keep fighting. Bielsa itself was largely destroyed. The village museum has a section on the pocket and the exodus.
look: A local museum with photographs, documents and objects about the Bielsa Pocket and the flight of civilians over the border.
plan: Bielsa is in the high Pyrenees, near the tunnel to France. Check the museum's seasonal opening times, and combine the visit with hiking in the valley.
disputed: The coordinates are the village centre, and the museum's exact spot was not verified. The dates and unit follow standard accounts because the museum's own page could not be read.

name: Caspe – battle of March 1938
text: From 1936 Caspe was the seat of the anarchist-led Regional Defence Council of Aragon, which ran the collectivised Republican part of the region. In August 1937 the Republican government dissolved the council by force and arrested its president, Joaquín Ascaso. During the Aragon offensive three divisions of Yagüe's Moroccan Army Corps reached Caspe on 15 March 1938. International Brigades XI, XIII and XV, later joined by the XII and XIV, defended the town, the XV Brigade most stubbornly. Caspe fell on 17 March and became a Nationalist corps headquarters for the Ebro front.
look: The historic town centre and the hills around the Guadalope valley where the brigades fought. Traces are scattered and mostly unmarked.
plan: Start from the old town and the tourist office. A local guide or book helps to locate the battle positions.

name: Fuentes de Ebro – tank attack of October 1937
text: As the last act of the Zaragoza offensive, the Republicans attacked the fortified town of Fuentes de Ebro, south-east of Zaragoza. A tank regiment of 48 Soviet-built BT-5s charged with XV International Brigade infantry riding on them or following behind, including the Canadian Mackenzie-Papineau Battalion in its first major action. Poorly coordinated with infantry and artillery, the attack broke down. Nineteen tanks and more than 300 men were lost, and the town stayed in Nationalist hands.
look: The open, flat fields where the attack went in. Visible remains are few.
plan: This stop is for enthusiasts. It is 25 km from Zaragoza on the way to Quinto and Belchite.
disputed: The attack date (13 Oct 1937) is the standard one but was not confirmed from a fetched source. Loss figures follow Wikipedia.

name: Aldehuela bunker
text: Before the Battle of Teruel the Popular Army built a fortified line south of the city facing Nationalist positions such as the Muela de Villaspesa. This concrete observation post on the hill opposite Aldehuela cemetery is one of the few pieces of that line to survive intact. From inside, observers could see Teruel itself.
look: A domed concrete bunker with stepped courses left by its formwork, entered through a tunnel on the slope.
plan: It is near the Teruel–Aldehuela road, about 10 km south-east of Teruel, and is freely accessible on foot. Take a torch.

name: Mansueto fort (Valdecebro)
text: Mansueto is a promontory guarding the south-eastern approach to Teruel above Valdecebro. The Republicans fortified it not with the usual sandbagged trenches but with a small fort of thick concrete and brick walls, roofed with a concrete slab on railway rails. It formed part of the Republican ring around Teruel.
look: Broken wall sections with firing loopholes and fragments of the concrete roof.
plan: It is a short walk from Valdecebro, about 5 km east of Teruel. The site is ruined, so watch your footing.

name: Las Viñas bunker (Teruel)
text: The Las Viñas sector around Teruel cemetery was contested from the very start of the war. A defence line on the ridge above the prison watched the Turia riverbed and the old Zaragoza road below the city. This concrete observation fort and bunker is one of its surviving pieces, on the edge of Teruel itself.
look: A thick-walled concrete fort used as an observatory, a rifle post and a bunker.
plan: It is on the Camino de Capuchinos near the cemetery, within walking distance of the centre. Visit together with the city sites.

name: Muela de Villaspesa
text: The Muela de Villaspesa was an intermediate fortified point south of Teruel overlooking the Republican positions at Aldehuela and the Turia valley. Its defenders dug a tunnel from the trench line to the back of the hill so they could move without being seen or hit from the Republican positions at Las Cañadas.
look: Trenches and observation posts on the slope facing Aldehuela, and the tunnel, whose rear entrance is now sealed.
plan: It is near Villaspesa, about 8 km south of Teruel. Open hillside, so bring boots. Combine it with the Aldehuela bunker opposite.
disputed: TracesOfWar does not say which side held the Muela. The layout suggests the Nationalists, but this is not confirmed.
